title: Mechanistic interpretability
summary:
Mechanistic interpretability (often abbreviated as mech interp, mechinterp, or MI) is a subfield of research within explainable artificial intelligence that aims to understand the internal workings of neural networks by analyzing the mechanisms present in their computations. The approach seeks to analyze neural networks in a manner similar to how binary computer programs can be reverse-engineered to understand their functions. The term was coined by Chris Olah.

Mechanistic interpretability aims to identify structures, circuits, or algorithms encoded in the weights of machine learning models. This contrasts with earlier interpretability methods that focused primarily on input-output explanations. Early work combined various techniques such as feature visualization, dimensionality reduction, and attribution with human-computer interaction methods to analyze models like the vision model Inception v1. Mechanistic interpretability employs causal methods to understand how internal model components influence outputs, often using formal tools from causality theory.

In the field of AI safety, mechanistic interpretability is used to understand and verify the behavior of complex AI systems, and to attempt to identify potential risks such as AI misalignment. Features refer to the specific properties or patterns that a neural network learns to recognize and process, while circuits are the pathways and computations that process this information. The relationship between features and circuits is hierarchical and interdependent.

Mechanistic interpretability seeks to reverse engineer neural networks, similar to how one might reverse engineer a compiled binary computer program. Neural network parameters are in some sense a binary computer program which runs on one of the exotic virtual machines we call a neural network architecture.
